cards.relevant: 这是气候变化导致物种分布改变的又一实证，提醒人们全球变暖正在重塑生态系统，外来物种可能威胁本地生物多样性。
cards.context: 黄蜂蜘蛛原本主要分布在欧洲大陆南部和中部，随着全球气温上升，其适宜栖息地逐渐向北扩展。英国此前仅在南部偶尔发现该物种，此次是首次在北部柴郡记录到。
cards.source_analysis: 《卫报》野生动物专栏报道，该媒体长期关注气候变化和生物多样性议题，立场倾向于强调环境危机的紧迫性。
cards.social_impact: 该发现是英国物种分布变化的缩影，反映出气候变暖正导致越来越多南方物种向北方迁移，可能改变当地生态平衡。
cards.source_text: She is an unlikely harbinger of the climate emergency: a venomous black and yellow spider who spins mysterious patterns in her webs and eats her mates for breakfast. Native to mainland Europe, north Africa and Asia, the Argiope bruennichi – commonly known as a wasp spider – is rarely seen in the north and west of Britain. But a fully grown female has been spotted in Cheshire for the first time by conservationists from Chester zoo, who stumbled across the large, brightly striped arachnid in a rewilded field. The species, which mimics a wasp to deter predators, is thought to be the latest “climate refugee” extending its range northwards as the planet heats. Females can grow to about 2cm in body length, making it one of the largest spiders found in the UK. “You know your big, chunky house spiders – the ones you think are massive and frighten the life out of you in your living room? A female wasp spider is probably a bit bigger than those,” said Scott Wilson, head of field programmes at the zoo. Although they are not dangerous to humans, they often attack and cannibalise their mates during or after copulation. Males usually reach only about a quarter of the length of the females and studies have found that up to 80% die after their first mating attempt while the rest die after their second. Their body then provides the female with valuable protein as she produces her eggs. It is not yet known how the spread of the wasp spider, which was also revealed to be moving west into counties such as Worcestershire, Herefordshire and Warwickshire last week, will affect local ecosystems in the north. “That’s quite often the risk with these ecological shifts – we don’t know what the implications will be,” said Wilson. The spider recorded in Cheshire was discovered on the Chester zoo estate during a routine “bioblitz” to monitor biodiversity on 80 hectares of land being set aside for nature. An expert from the British Arachnological Society later confirmed it was the first recorded sighting of the species in the county. “It was quite easy to spot,” said Wilson. “It’s a really big, colourful spider and the webs are huge and distinctive … They have this thick zigzag, which some people think is there to reflect UV light and attract insects, but nobody really knows.” The wider zoo estate, which includes wet meadows,grasslands, woodlands and orchards, already supports a diverse range of important UK species, such as great crested newts, badgers and harvest mice. cards.context: 北极永久冻土储存了大量有机碳，气候变暖导致冻土解冻，改变地表水文条件，进而影响湖泊的存亡。此前缺乏对北极湖泊的系统性编目。

cards.social_impact: 北极湖泊的变化直接影响当地生态系统和原住民社区的水源与生计，同时冻土融化释放的甲烷和二氧化碳对全球气候有反馈效应。
cards.source_text: The Arctic is dotted with millions of lakes that sit on persistently frozen soil called permafrost. These lakes are crucial for the region’s wildlife and local communities. However, as temperatures rise, the permafrost thaws, which causes new lakes to form or existing lakes to abruptly disappear as lake water drains away through newly created channels. Researchers have now created an interactive map called Lost Lakes that allows people to monitor changes in around 4 million Arctic lakes in near real time. It can also show how the lakes have changed since 2016. Monitoring lake dynamics can offer important clues for the underlying permafrost, the researchers say. “LostLakes is completely free and designed to be used by experts and non-experts at the same time,” Ingmar Nitze, a remote sensing researcher at Germany’s Alfred Wegener Institute, which helped create the database, told Mongabay by email. Much of the Arctic’s ground sits on ice-rich permafrost. Over hundreds and thousands of years, this permafrost has accumulated massive amounts of carbon as plant, animal and microbe matter got trapped in the frozen soil. However, as the Arctic warms faster than the global average due to climate change, much of the region’s permafrost is thawing. “Once the permafrost thaws, some of this carbon, which was freeze-locked there for thousands of years, can go to the atmosphere and further fuel the warming, which may lead to a faster permafrost thaw,” Nitze said. Permafrost itself is challenging to monitor directly at large scale because it lies beneath the ground and researchers typically dig into it for measurements. However, the lakes, which often form or disappear with changes in the underlying permafrost, can be easily monitored by satellite imagery. When the ground temperature rises above freezing (0° Celsius, or 32° Fahrenheit), ice starts to thaw, causing the ground to sink and water to collect. This forms a pool, which over years and centuries can become a lake, Nitze said. “In west Alaska we have some ponds that started forming in the mid 20th century. Many Arctic lakes started forming around 12,000 years ago.” As more surrounding permafrost thaws, channels can appear through which water can drain out of lakes. In northwestern Alaska, for instance, nearly 200 lakes shrank in the summer of 2018, following an unusually warm winter, Nitze and Anna Liljedahl of the University of Alaska Fairbanks wrote in The Conversation. cards.context: 秘鲁安第斯山脉的冰川近年来因气候变化加速退缩，导致下游社区水源减少。当地社区结合祖传的生态管理智慧，尝试修复退化的高地湿地和草原，以增强水源涵养。

cards.source_text: A new atlas of biodiversity of the Galápagos Islands highlights the unique evolutionary and ecological diversity of life in the famed archipelago that helped Charles Darwin develop the theory of natural selection. The Galapagos Atlas, created by the Darwin Foundation, highlights 68 species and species groups in the island chain. These include the celebrities of Galápagos biodiversity, such as the giant tortoises (genus Chelonoidis), marine iguanas (Amblyrhynchus cristatus), and Darwin finches (genus Geospiza). It also features less famous plants and animals, such as the Galápagos kelp (Eisenia galapagensis), lichens, and Galápagos carpenter bees (Xylocopa darwini). The freely available atlas was created by a team of 87 authors and artists including scientists, park rangers, and conservationists. Profiles of every species highlight both what’s known about them, but also what still remains unknown about their ecology, behavior, and conservation needs. “There is still so much we don’t fully understand about Galapagos flora and fauna, and that’s part of what makes it so fascinating,” Darwin Foundation executive director Rakan Zahawi told Mongabay by email. Zahawi called the Galapagos Atlas a starting point for people wanting to solve some of the scientific mysteries of life in the islands. “Each species entry comes with citations and references, so my first piece of advice to a young person who’s captivated by a species is to follow those leads,” he added. “Dig into the research behind the entry, see who’s been studying it and what they’ve found, and let that pull you further into the subject.” The Galapagos Atlas also includes primers on the natural history, human history, ecology, evolution, and geology of the Galápagos Islands. Furthermore, it highlights animals and plants that have become invasive to the islands. “Galapagos today has around 1,500 introduced species, of which just over 60 are classified as invasive, meaning they’re throwing the ecosystems out of balance and impacting native flora and fauna,” Zahawi said. He added he hopes the atlas will raise the awareness needed to keep other potentially invasive species from reaching the Galápagos in the first place. “The picture could be far worse: Galapagos authorities do strong work controlling entries into the archipelago, but every bit helps, and the more tourists understand their own potential to accidentally introduce a species, the better our odds of preventing it.” Galapagos Atlas editor-in-chief

cards.source_text: Critical theorists like Theodor Adorno may have overreached in claiming that all mass culture is mediocre, mechanized propaganda made to justify the status quo. But that doesn’t mean they were entirely wrong. Over and over we see even the most subversive art, literature, film, and music has a way of being tamed and Bowdlerized. Global mega-corporate industries don’t need to censor what they don’t like; they only need to buy it, rebrand it, or price it out of reach. So what? Why do we need challenging, independent art when we have endless entertainment? Is the concept a nostalgic, elitist, Eurocentric idea? Artists have justified the need for art since antiquity, with poetic and logical arguments of every kind. But Dada artists of the early 20th century broke ranks, building their movement on the insight that no defense could possibly mean anything when it came to art’s purpose, especially in the face of the technocratic slaughter of World War I. When the hyperrationalism of modernity led to mass death and destruction, the only humane response was to declare war on rationalization—to “destroy the hoaxes of reason,” as French artist Jean Arp put it. “For the disillusioned artists of the Dada movement,” the Museum of Modern Art explains, “the war merely confirmed the degradation of social structures that led to such violence: corrupt and nationalist politics, repressive social values, and unquestioning conformity of culture and thought.” Dada took a combative stance against, for one thing, the insistence that art justify its existence to win establishment approval. “All activity is vain,” declared poet Tristan Tzara in his 1918 “Dada Manifesto,” including the “monetary system, pharmaceutical product, or a bare leg advertising the ardent sterile spring…. The beginnings of Dada were not the beginnings of art, but of disgust” with the ossified culture of the “nice, nice bourgeois,” who would preserve at any cost “the possibility of wallowing in cushions and good things to eat.” “And so Dada,” wrote Tzara, “was born of a need for independence, of a distrust toward unity.” Such declarations aside, the movement was decidedly unified in its aims. “For us, art is not an end in itself,” poet Hugo Ball wrote. “It is an opportunity for the true perception and criticism of the times we live in.” This critique required new experimental techniques that deformed and repurposed the technologies of mass culture. cards.source_text: Many a foreigner has visited England and found it an unexpectedly surreal place. Some of that effect has to do with encountering familiar icons — Big Ben, double-decker Routemaster buses, Marmite — in cold, damp reality. More of it may be induced by the country’s simultaneously thoroughgoing cultures of normality and eccentricity, an endless source of inspiration for Monty Python’s Flying Circus and much other British comedy since. Yet England came relatively late to Surrealism, or rather, Surrealism came late to England. When the International Surrealist Exhibition opened at the New Burlington Galleries behind London’s Royal Academy in the summer of 1936, the Manchester Evening News decried it as “a travesty of everything that’s decent.” Naturally, the show was a smash hit. On display was work by artists including Pablo Picasso, René Magritte, Max Ernst, Alexander Calder, Giorgio de Chirico, Marcel Duchamp, Alberto Giacometti, Paul Klee, Man Ray, and Salvador Dalí, who turned up in person to deliver a lecture on “Authentic Paranoiac Phantoms.” In order to “descend to the subconscious” with a properly Surrealist literalism, he rented a diving suit and helmet from a local outfitter for his appearance. (You can see an actual image from 1936 here.) “The diving suit had extremely heavy lead shoes which I could barely lift,” he writes in his autobiography, as translated by Haakon Chevalier. “I therefore had to walk very slowly, leaning on friends who helped to move me, as though I were completely paralyzed, and thus I appeared before the audience holding two luxurious white Russian wolfhounds on a leash.” Only after he’d been talking for a few minutes did Dalí realize that “it would be impossible for me to deliver my speech through the glass window of my helmet. cards.source_text: The North Sea, with its cold grey waters, is the world’s drabbest. Or so you might have thought, but this documentary featuring the Dutch diver and underwater cinematographer Peter van Rodijnen sets out to tackle the misconceptions. His stunning footage puts all the splendours of this stormy stretch of water on show, and his voiceover gives it an endearing eccentric charm. First, the greyness. Van Rodijnen films the North Sea’s waves sparkling with the cosmic blue light of bioluminescent algae, and lit up with the disco colours of coral and plankton blooms. He also brings us cute, coo-worthy stories from the depths; take the male shorthorn sculpin fish (no looker, it must be said) who spends the winter looking after his eggs, cleaning and blowing fresh water over them. Van Rodijnen’s camera is there for the baby fish hatching – pop, pop, pop out of their pearly plump pink eggs. There are some quirky stories, too, including a barnacle with a superlong penis. Other moments are pure spectacle. A teeming school of mackerel puts on an Olympic show of synchronised swimming, and Rodijnen’s patience as a film-maker pays off with jaw-dropping footage, literally in the case of a basking shark filmed off the coast of Scotland. Swimming with its mouth open, feeding on plankton, it’s “the big friendly giant of the seas”, says Van Rodijnen. But it can’t be a nature documentary unless there is an environmental catastrophe on the horizon. In Scotland, numbers of a puffin breeding colony are down by 30% due to overfishing. But there are eco wins, too. The Atlantic bluefin tuna, which vanished from the North Sea in the 1960s, is back, and it’s a brute – it can grow heavier than a grand piano. What the film lacks in slickness, it makes up for with enthusiasm.
cards.source_title: North Sea, Nature Untamed review – stunning footage finds the beauty and splendour under the water

Isn’t it all in the past? Weren’t we the first to abolish it anyway? In April, the Reform party announced a new policy of halting visas to people from countries seeking slavery reparations from Britain. “The United Kingdom is not an ATM for ethnic grievances from the past,” the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said. Unfortunately for those who would rather forget, the slave trade, as William Pettigrew argues in this grimly important book, can be found “in the depths of Britain’s grain”. Ninety per cent of the enslaved Africans transported to America went on British ships, and slave traders’ actions transformed Britain in ways that still resonate today. The erasure of this history began with the abolitionists, who quickly realised that identifying and shaming slave traders might harm their cause. They chose instead to argue that abolition would confirm Britain’s superior moral righteousness. Lauding abolition obscured what Pettigrew calls “slave gain”: Britain’s gigantic profiting from the trade. Wilkie Collins and Charles Dickens, in a jointly authored article of 1857, blithely suggested that the gains of slavery had evaporated “as the Arabian Wizard’s money turned to leaves”. Thus began a general tendency to downplay Britain’s role, offshoring slavery’s causes and effects to the Americas or localising them to port cities such as Bristol and Liverpool. Since April 2021, Pettigrew has led a group of nine academic historians identifying all the known investors – about 13,000 of them – who financed Britain’s brutal trafficking of 3.3 million enslaved Africans, of whom about half a million died during the Atlantic crossing. After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, English slave merchants loosened their ties with the monarchy and embraced a free market. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 28 minute listen In late summer 2023, I found myself in a smoke shop looking at a package of ‘magic mushroom’ gummies. That phrase, magic mushrooms, usually calls to mind one type of mushroom: those containing psilocybin, the compound showing promise as a therapy for depression, addiction and other psychopathologies. But these gummies were not psilocybin. Instead, the packaging described Amanita muscaria, the red-capped, white-spotted toadstool of fairy-tale forests, iPhone keyboards and Super Mario. I knew a little about the folklore of Amanita muscaria. I had first seen it discussed in an episode of the show Hamilton’s Pharmacopeia (2016-21), which begins with a claim I now hear often: that Amanita muscaria may be among the oldest human intoxicants. The New York banker-turned-ethnomycologist R Gordon Wasson, whose Life magazine essay from 1957 introduced psilocybin mushrooms to a mass Western audience, certainly took this idea seriously. In his book Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968), he argued that the Vedic soma – a ritual drink in ancient Indian religions – was made from Amanita muscaria. The mushroom has also been linked, sometimes carefully and sometimes wildly, to the origins of Santa Claus, Viking berserkers and even Christianity. cards.source_text: For Abidin, a Balik elder who lives in East Kalimantan in Borneo, Indonesia, the sounds of nature aren’t merely a backdrop but a vital part of how he navigates the world. But as the rainforest around him has become more developed, the calls of creatures once heard everywhere have grown scarce. And that process is speeding up. To relieve Indonesia’s capital city of Jakarta, which is sinking due to overdevelopment and vulnerable to climate change, the government is building a new one, Nusantara, close to Abidin’s home. The noise of construction and city life is beginning to overpower the soundscape he relies on, and researchers suspect they may already be pushing wildlife away. In this short documentary, the US director Leah Varjacques traces an effort to record the sounds of the rainforest before they’re altered forever. The film follows Abidin working with a research team that includes Wendy Erb, a bioacoustic scientist from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in New York, to collect audio from caves, treetops and everywhere in between. cards.source_text: It is rare for me to visit the same place twice within a couple of weeks, but my walk in the Teifi Marshes recently was curtailed by heavy rain, and I feel that I have unfinished business. Last time I started from the Cilgerran end of the marsh, so today begin at the seaward side – crossing the bridge over the Teifi and heading upstream past the site of the old, sadly long-departed Cardigan railway station. My route follows the former course of the railway line, but I briefly divert along a boardwalk into the broad reedbeds at the heart of the marsh. Here, I am surrounded by the ambient sound of the wind in the reeds, which ebbs and flows with an almost animate organic static – pushing back the distant sounds of traffic on the main road. Scrub and small trees interact with the reeds at the margins, their autumn bounty of fruits already well advanced. The blackberries are almost over, but the sloes are plump and mature with the promise of a warming winter spirit to come. Back on the main trail, a weasel, a low blur of fur and legs, dashes across the path in front of me just as the sun emerges from banks of grey cloud. The new shadows make me look up. Beyond the mile or so of reedbed, the valley side is wooded with deciduous trees just beginning to fade into autumn colours. Among them, a few bare crowns of what I take to be dead ash trees stand skeletal, awaiting the winter storm The Afon Teifi is tidal here, and it is about an hour after high water. The level in the creek off the main channel is starting to fall, exposing freshly wetted mud. Along the edge of the water, a pair of dunlin explore what the receding tide has left on offer, hunting with their short bills and jerky movements, while nearby ducks take a more leisurely approach. On my last visit, I caught a glimpse of a kingfisher from this spot, but today it is absent – as is the heron I had hoped to get a better picture of. Next time, perhaps. Next time.

That’s true of the songs themselves—which might be 20-minute slabs of ambient-leaning electronics or one-minute gasps of sharp, diffident funk—and for the way he releases them, with full LP campaigns punctuated by breadcrumb trails, short films, and download-only albums in between. His music follows its own strange, self-referential logic: Track titles are only vaguely comprehensible, and conceptual inspirations like chess and Milton’s Paradise Lost are flattened into his bit-crushed, hermetically-sealed sound world. The artist born Darren Cunningham is one of the most instantly recognizable electronic producers going, with a style—lo-fi, filtered, looping, limping—that has served him well for over 20 years. Enter Radical Frame, his 10th album. It’s brittle and uneven, beginning with two songs under 30 seconds long and ending with a 16-minute collaboration with Manchester rapper-poet Rainy Miller. Radical Frame is good, but it makes you work for it. The album is immediately disorienting. The first track is a manipulated voice saying “The Experiment,” stretching across the stereo spectrum as though it were being squeezed through a sieve. That’s followed by a five-second tune with a deep voice intoning,“Gimme the fuckin money, man.” From there it swings into one of the most brutal Actress tracks in recent memory: “Live By You” begins as a hard-edged yet melancholy UK rap track with CASISDEAD before Cunningham throws the whole thing down the garbage disposal, with rapidfire handclaps and harsh static swallowing up the MC’s voice. It’s transcendent; it’s hilarious. During my first viewing, I cackled so loudly during this scene I worried one of my neighbors would report me. If fewer viewers remember Alex G’s score, that’s a testament to his mindmeld with Schoenbrun. He has scored all their films, and by now his cues melt into the shadows of Schoenbrun’s work. The pair are kindred souls: They’re both critical darlings whose influences don’t enjoy critical-darling status. Alex G has reverently name-dropped Audioslave; Schoenbrun grew up loving nu-metal. Teenage Sex and Death is their complicated valentine to cruddy ’80s slasher franchises like Friday the 13th and Sleepaway Camp. No score yet, be the first to add. Alex G’s records are steeped in the ephemera of music making, and the mix overflows with little tactile cues that signify the creative process: impressions of warped vinyl, babbled and sampling voices that connote studio chatter, guitars quietly noodling away. His music is appealing on its surface, but the reason he haunts people, pulls them into his orbit, is that his music feels like it’s making itself, like he’s steeped in his own creation, at the moment you listen. This is kind of how Schoenbrun makes films—they are in thrall to the power that media can have over a psyche, and their movies are basically paeans to what happens when people gaze into screens and discover portals out of themselves. Alex G and Schoenbrun are so attuned that their successes and misfires tend to line up—what works in the music is what works in the movie, and vice versa. The fingerpicked acoustic guitar and shimmering synthesizers that tag along after Hannah Einbinder’s wide-eyed ingénue on “DVD Rack” and “Dipping” telegraph that Miasma is largely redemptive. cards.source_text: Good morning, “Britain” was a centuries-long sociological study conducted by imperial grifters. In 2012, it came to an end; the country thanked us all for our participation in its great and terrible colonial project. The funeral took place at the London Olympics that year, and the ghost of Britain soon came rolling out on a Union Jack hovercraft. A new generation of artists has since scooped ooze from the zombie, venturing into a memory of Britain they were barely old enough to experience themselves: from PinkPantheress’ cool but campy vision of pre-austerity Britain to Jim Legxacy’s dreamy historiography of Black British music. Growing up down the road from Legxacy, 27-year-old newcomer Kamal Frederick, aka BEASTIE, figuratively and spiritually shares his lane, taking the stoic futurist music of the British early aughts—grime, drill, trap—and making it wistful and aching. No score yet, be the first to add. Raised on the edge of South London in Mitcham—supposedly one of England’s most haunted towns—BEASTIE became a teenage fan of vaguely alternative, mood-heavy artists like Interpol, Frank Ocean, and Dev Hynes, while his schoolmates listened almost exclusively to drill and grime. Again, like Jim Legxacy (whose comparison is difficult to shirk at this early stage in his career), BEASTIE became artistically interested in what could happen when he filtered the tough, local sounds of grime through more generalized and introverted genres like indie bedroom pop and sensual R&B. On maria, his second EP, BEASTIE looks back on his coming-of-age in Mitcham and the Black culture surrounding and informing it. The nine tracks are, fittingly for Mitcham, spectral and grimly psychedelic, folding the haze of his inner world into the sounds that raised him. Lead single “Mitcham Mint” takes its name from a particularly run-down local pub and beautifies it, as memory is wont to do, with dream-pop guitars, sliding harmonies, and a feeling of music spinning in several directions at once while somehow finding its footing. It is a devotional exercise in atmosphere, faithful to the alt influences on which he was raised. Across the EP, the percussion is crunchy, dry, and distorted, while BEASTIE’s voice floats above, bubble-like and lovely. On “Does It Rain?” BEASTIE’s treatment of grime influences and samples feels like a memory of a memory of a memory. cards.source_text: In Spike Lee’s 2000 stand-up showcase The Original Kings of Comedy, Steve Harvey has a Black-famous segment reminiscing on the days when “music was music.” On stage, he transports the rowdy crowd back to the mid-1970s, the era of yearning soul ballads that felt so deeply real they could send a tingle through your entire body. He makes his point by blasting a few examples: The sweet vocal harmonies of Earth, Wind & Fire’s “Would You Mind” gets people hitting doo-wop snaps in the aisles; the opening drum roll of the Ohio Players’ “I Want to Be Free” morphs into an orgasmic choir of screams; and the begging hook of Lenny Williams’ “’Cause I Love You” turns into panties on the stage and Steve Harvey Chun-Li kicking a stool. “Boy, this motherfucker sangin’ this song,” says Steve, as he dives into a hilariously cranky rant about what modern music is missing. If I were to stage my own version of Harvey’s bit today, I’d be looking back at the bluesy hustle rappers who used to be synonymous with Southern hip-hop. I’m thinking Pimp C, who could go from sounding like the lead singer of a funk band to laying down unfiltered verses of straight pimpsploitation. Or maybe Big Moe, who sang-rapped like an ex-church boy turned high-roller. And now we have the country-fried D-boy raps of Fetty P Franklin, a Charlotte storyteller who sounds like he means every word that comes out of his mouth. For years now, he’s been scraping together autobiographical and darkly funny memories (“My uncle used to give me brown liquor when I was wearin’ Pampers,” he raps on “Paper Cups,” off the deluxe edition of FRANK, the 2025 tape that blew his music up to another level) of the project-housing environment that shaped him into the sort of guy who could “make a thousand quicker than I can make a salad.” It’s old school go-getter rap where nostalgia is part of the appeal but doesn’t feel like the schtick. items.title: Britain’s Slave Traders by William A Pettigrew review – the inconvenient truth
items.summary: This revelatory history shows just how deeply embedded slavery is in the foundations of modern Britain One tedious aspect of Britain’s post-imperial melancholia is the number of amateur historians who would rather we stopped going on about our role in the slave trade. Isn’t it all in the past? Weren’t we the first to abolish it anyway? In April, the Reform party announced a new policy of halting visas to people from countries seeking slavery reparations from Britain. “The United Kingdom is not an ATM for ethnic grievances from the past,” the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said. Unfortunately for those who would rather forget, the slave trade, as William Pettigrew argues in this grimly important book, can be found “in the depths of Britain’s grain”. Ninety per cent of the enslaved Africans transported to America went on British ships, and slave traders’ actions transformed Britain in ways that still resonate today. Continue reading...

items.title: The Complex by Karan Mahajan review – a superb family saga set in Delhi
items.summary: At once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty differences, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with drama We learn about the murder of the Chopra clan’s shifty, crude, charismatic patriarch Laxman in the opening pages of The Complex. Twenty-five years have passed, but the stain on this once-respectable Punjabi family remains. The man who did it, Laxman’s nephew Brij, has served his jail time and is about to be released. Some relatives think Brij is too dangerous, too shameful to return to the family home, but his son Mohit decides the pair will live together – and rewinds the clock to tell the story of the decades leading up to the crime. Karan Mahajan’s warmly received first two works, Family Planning and The Association of Small Bombs , explored individual lives alongside larger forces – urban development in the former, a car bomb’s traumatic aftermath in the latter. His excellent third novel has Delhi at its heart, but also visits Indian villages and cities, the American midwest and London, its short chapters flitting between different members of the Chopra family. You start by nodding in appreciation at Mahajan’s observant character portraits; before you know it you’re waist-deep in frustration, corruption and betrayal, as the book ranges through politics, faith, migration, infidelity and entrepreneurship. Or so you might have thought, but this documentary featuring the Dutch diver and underwater cinematographer Peter van Rodijnen sets out to tackle the misconceptions. His stunning footage puts all the splendours of this stormy stretch of water on show, and his voiceover gives it an endearing eccentric charm. First, the greyness. Van Rodijnen films the North Sea’s waves sparkling with the cosmic blue light of bioluminescent algae, and lit up with the disco colours of coral and plankton blooms. items.title: Country diary: An autumn bounty of fruits is well on its way | John Gilbey
items.summary: Cardigan: Taking a walk beside the River Teifi, I encounter trees beginning to fade into new season colour, and the low blur of a weasel It is rare for me to visit the same place twice within a couple of weeks, but my walk in the Teifi Marshes recently was curtailed by heavy rain, and I feel that I have unfinished business. Last time I started from the Cilgerran end of the marsh, so today begin at the seaward side – crossing the bridge over the Teifi and heading upstream past the site of the old, sadly long-departed Cardigan railway station . My route follows the former course of the railway line, but I briefly divert along a boardwalk into the broad reedbeds at the heart of the marsh. Here, I am surrounded by the ambient sound of the wind in the reeds, which ebbs and flows with an almost animate organic static – pushing back the distant sounds of traffic on the main road. Scrub and small trees interact with the reeds at the margins, their autumn bounty of fruits already well advanced. The blackberries are almost over, but the sloes are plump and mature with the promise of a warming winter spirit to come. Continue reading...
